questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A bank wants to discover natural groups among its customers based on spending behavior. It has no predefined segments and no labels. Which approach should the data team use?
options: Supervised classification, which learns from labeled examples of segments overall.
Regression, which predicts a number from the past data of customers
Fine-tuning a foundation model on the data of the bank
Unsupervised learning (clustering), which finds groups without any labels
questions.correct_rationale: With no labels, the goal is to find structure the business doesn't know yet.
questions.distractor_summary: Clustering, a form of unsupervised learning, groups similar customers together. Classification and regression are supervised and need known outcomes to learn from, and fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model to a task. It isn't a segmentation method.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A contact center wants to use AI on its call recordings, customer emails, and scanned PDF complaint letters. What type of data are these?
options: Unstructured data, which has no fixed schema or format
Structured data, which sits in rows and columns of tables
Time-series data, which is a series of values over time
Labeled data, where each record has a known answer overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Audio, free text, and scanned documents don't fit neatly into rows and columns, so they're unstructured.
questions.distractor_summary: Unstructured data is where generative AI and language models add a lot of value. Structured data lives in tables, time-series data is ordered by time, and "labeled" describes whether known answers are attached, not the format.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A fraud model gives a transaction a fraud score of 0.82. The operations manager asks what this means for the business. Which response is most accurate?
options: The transaction is definitely fraudulent and so must always be blocked
The model is 82% accurate overall across all of the predictions it makes
The score has no meaning until the model has been retrained once again
It's a probability-style estimate; the business picks a threshold balancing missed fraud and blocked customers
questions.correct_rationale: ML outputs are probabilistic, not certain.
questions.distractor_summary: Setting the decision threshold is a business choice. A lower threshold catches more fraud but blocks more legitimate customers (more false positives). A higher threshold lets more fraud through (more false negatives). A single score says nothing about the model's overall accuracy.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A vendor's lead-scoring model is 98% accurate on its training data but only 70% accurate on new leads after go-live. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Overfitting: the model memorized the training data and doesn't generalize
Underfitting: the model is too simple to learn the patterns
Hallucination: the model is inventing leads that don't exist in production.
Inference latency: the model is responding too slowly to the sales team overall.
questions.correct_rationale: High accuracy on training data combined with much lower accuracy on unseen data is the classic sign of overfitting.
questions.distractor_summary: Business leaders should ask for performance on held-out or real-world data, not just training results. Underfitting shows poor results on both, hallucination is a generative AI behavior, and latency is about speed, not accuracy.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A card issuer's fraud team maintains more than 2,000 hand-written rules. Fraudsters change tactics weekly, and the rules can't keep up. Why is machine learning a better fit here?
options: ML removes the need for any human fraud analysts on the team in production.
ML guarantees that the issuer will have zero fraud losses
ML is always cheaper to run than a set of rules
ML learns complex, changing patterns that are impractical to code by hand
questions.correct_rationale: ML is valuable when patterns are too complex or change too fast for hand-written rules.
questions.distractor_summary: It still needs monitoring, retraining, and human review. No model guarantees zero losses, and ML isn't automatically cheaper, because data, training, and operations all cost money.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A hotel chain receives 30,000 online reviews a month and wants to know whether guests feel positive or negative about cleanliness, staff, and price. Which AI capability fits?
options: Natural language processing (sentiment analysis) of the reviews
Computer vision, which analyzes the photos that guests post overall.
Anomaly detection on the sensor data from the hotels for the team.
Reinforcement learning, where an agent learns from rewards overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Sentiment analysis is an NLP task that classifies the emotional tone of text, and it can be broken down by topic.
questions.distractor_summary: A pre-trained managed service such as Amazon Comprehend can do this without building a custom model. The other options deal with images, sensor streams, and trial-and-error learning.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A lender wants to automate approvals for small-business loans. Regulators require the lender to give every declined applicant specific reasons for the decision. Which consideration should most influence the choice of solution?
options: Choose whichever model has the highest accuracy, however it decides in every region.
Use a generative AI model to write persuasive rejection letters
Prioritize explainability, with an interpretable model or rules for each decision
Avoid documenting the model's logic to protect intellectual property in production.
questions.correct_rationale: When decisions affect people and regulators require reasons, explainability is a hard requirement.
questions.distractor_summary: Sometimes it's worth giving up a little accuracy for a model, or a rules-plus-ML approach, whose decisions can be traced. A persuasive letter isn't a real explanation, and hiding the logic undermines compliance and trust.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: An insurer's claims leader asks for "generative AI to estimate the dollar cost of each new auto claim." What should an AI business strategist recommend?
options: Use generative AI, because it can handle any kind of AI task, including this one
Treat it as a regression problem for ML, with generative AI to summarize notes
Avoid AI entirely, because claims involve money and strict regulation
Use computer vision alone, because cost estimates come only from photos
questions.correct_rationale: Estimating a number from historical outcomes is a prediction (regression) task, where traditional ML tends to be more accurate, consistent, cheaper, and easier to explain.
questions.distractor_summary: Generative AI can still add value alongside it, for example by summarizing adjuster notes. Matching the type of AI to the problem, not to the hype, is what this exam tests.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A COO asks how an "AI agent" differs from the FAQ chatbot already on the company website. Which answer is most accurate?
options: An agent is a chatbot with a more natural-sounding voice across the subscriptions.
An agent only works with structured data, while chatbots use text for the team.
An agent plans multi-step tasks and takes actions in other systems with tools
An agent is a chatbot that never needs any human oversight for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: The defining traits of an agent are a goal, the ability to plan steps, and tool use.
questions.distractor_summary: For example, an agent can look up an order, issue a return label, and update the CRM. A chatbot responds to questions. Voice and data type don't define an agent, and agents need *more* oversight than chatbots, not less, because they take actions.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A retailer is deploying a customer-service agent that can issue refunds. Leadership wants speed but is worried about large mistakes. Which design best balances value and risk?
options: Let the agent refund up to a set limit, and require human approval above it
Let the agent issue any refund on its own to maximize the speed for the team.
Require human approval for every refund, even the $3 ones for the application.
Don't allow agents near financial actions under any circumstances by default.
questions.correct_rationale: Matching how much the agent can do alone to the risk of the action is the core agent-governance principle.
questions.distractor_summary: Low-value, reversible actions can be automated, and high-impact ones need a human in the loop. Full autonomy takes on unnecessary risk, approving every refund wipes out the value, and a blanket ban gives up a sound use case.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A sales assistant agent must check live inventory in the company's ERP system before it quotes delivery dates. What capability makes this possible?
options: A larger context window for the model of the sales assistant at this stage.
Fine-tuning the model on the inventory data of last year
A higher temperature setting for the model of the assistant in the near term.
Tool use (function calling) through an approved API to the ERP system
questions.correct_rationale: Agents reach live systems by calling tools such as APIs, databases, and business applications.
questions.distractor_summary: A context window holds text the model is given, not live data. Fine-tuning on old inventory would produce stale answers, and temperature controls how varied the wording is.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: An email-triage agent can read incoming messages and send emails on staff's behalf. A security review finds that a malicious incoming email could contain hidden instructions telling the agent to forward confidential files outside the company. Which response best addresses this risk?
options: Raise the model's temperature so it ignores any instructions inside of emails for this team.
Shut down all of the AI use across the entire company at once
Limit permissions, add guardrails, and require approval before sensitive data is sent out
Fine-tune the model on more examples of the emails of the staff
questions.correct_rationale: This is prompt injection, which is especially dangerous for agents that can take actions.
questions.distractor_summary: Layered controls reduce both the chance of an attack succeeding and the damage it can do: least privilege, input and output guardrails, and approval steps for high-impact actions. Temperature and fine-tuning don't address the threat, and a blanket shutdown is disproportionate.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: An HR team wants employees to get instant answers about the benefits handbook. Nothing in the process needs to be changed in other systems. A vendor proposes an autonomous multi-agent platform. What should an AI business strategist recommend?
options: Accept the multi-agent platform, because agents are the newest technology throughout the organization overall.
Build a custom foundation model for the HR team throughout the organization across the subscriptions overall.
Use rule-based automation, because AI can't answer questions throughout the organization for the application.
Start with a simpler assistant grounded in the handbook (RAG), and add agents only if actions are needed
questions.correct_rationale: Agents add complexity, cost, and risk that are only justified when the task needs actions or multi-step work.
questions.distractor_summary: Answering questions from documents is a classic RAG job. The exam rewards choosing the simplest option that meets the need, not the newest technology. A custom model is overkill, and rules can't handle open-ended questions well.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A travel company's booking agent will remember each customer's seat and meal preferences across future conversations. Which business consideration does this memory feature raise most directly?
options: The need for a larger GPU cluster to store the preferences of customers by default.
Data privacy, consent, and retention policies for the stored customer information
Switching to unsupervised learning for the booking agent of the company by default.
Removing the need for a privacy notice on the booking site across the subscriptions.
questions.correct_rationale: Agent memory is stored personal data.
questions.distractor_summary: The business needs a lawful basis or consent, clear retention limits, a way for customers to delete their data, and access controls. Hardware and learning type aren't the issue, and memory makes a privacy notice *more* necessary, not less.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A manufacturer's procurement agent will negotiate routine reorders directly with suppliers' AI agents. What should leadership define before allowing this agent-to-agent interaction?
options: Authority limits, escalation rules, and who is accountable for the agreed outcomes
Nothing, because agents that negotiate with agents carry no business risk as a result.
Only the temperature setting of the model that the agent uses
A policy that suppliers must use the same AI vendor as the manufacturer over time in practice.
questions.correct_rationale: When agents act for the business with outside parties, governance has to define what the agent may commit to, when a person takes over, and who owns the result.
questions.distractor_summary: Agent-to-agent deals create real contractual and financial exposure. Temperature is a minor technical setting, and requiring the same vendor isn't realistic or relevant.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A marketing team's generative AI drafts are too formal and don't follow the brand's style. What should the team try first?
options: Fine-tune a model on 10,000 documents that the brand has published as needed.
Improve the prompts with tone instructions, brand rules, and sample outputs
Build a custom model from scratch just for the marketing team
Abandon generative AI for marketing work until the tools improve for the team.
questions.correct_rationale: Prompt engineering is the cheapest and fastest way to customize a model, so it comes first.
questions.distractor_summary: Instructions, a system prompt with brand rules, and examples often fix tone. Fine-tuning and custom models cost far more and are justified only if better prompting falls short.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A legal-ops team pastes an entire 200-page contract into every question it asks a generative AI tool, and the monthly bill is far higher than expected. The service charges per input and output token. Which change would cut cost the most while keeping answers useful?
options: Ask longer, more detailed questions about the contract each time by default.
Switch to a larger model that costs more for each token
Raise the temperature setting so that the answers get shorter
Send only the relevant sections, for example retrieved with RAG, each time
questions.correct_rationale: Token-based pricing means input size drives cost.
questions.distractor_summary: Sending only the relevant passages cuts tokens sharply and often improves focus. Longer prompts and larger models raise cost, and temperature has no effect on token pricing.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A field-service company wants technicians to ask questions about a 600-page equipment manual. The manual is longer than the model's context window. What is the most practical approach?
options: Use RAG to retrieve and send only the manual sections that are relevant
Wait for a model that has an unlimited context window for the application.
Shorten the manual to 20 pages so that it fits in the model for the team.
Train a new foundation model on the manual from scratch for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: The context window caps how much text a model can consider at once.
questions.distractor_summary: RAG works around it by indexing the manual, often as embeddings in a vector store, and retrieving only the relevant chunks per question. Waiting or cutting the manual isn't practical, and training a foundation model is extremely costly and unnecessary.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A bank's internal assistant must answer staff questions about lending policies. The policies change weekly, and compliance requires every answer to show which policy document it came from. Which approach fits best?
options: Fine-tune the model on the policies every week of the year for the application.
Use a general model that has no access to the policies
Use retrieval-augmented generation over the current policies, with citations
Use continued pre-training on textbooks about the banking industry by default.
questions.correct_rationale: RAG pulls current documents at question time, so updates take effect without retraining, and answers can cite their sources, which compliance needs.
questions.distractor_summary: Weekly fine-tuning is costly and can't easily cite sources. A general model doesn't know internal policies, and textbooks don't contain this bank's rules.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A medical-coding vendor needs a model to produce outputs in a highly specialized format and terminology across millions of records. Careful prompting and examples still give inconsistent formatting. The underlying knowledge rarely changes, and the vendor has thousands of high-quality labeled examples. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Switch to RAG, because RAG fixes the problems with formatting
Fine-tune a foundation model on the labeled examples
Raise the temperature to get more variety in the outputs
Go back to manual coding for all of the records
questions.correct_rationale: Fine-tuning fits when you need consistent *behavior*, such as format, style, or domain-specific output, that prompting can't deliver, and you have quality labeled data.
questions.distractor_summary: RAG adds knowledge rather than shaping behavior, higher temperature makes outputs less consistent, and going back to manual coding gives up the efficiency gains.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A sales team complains that the company's generative AI assistant "doesn't know" about a product launched last month and asks IT to "fix the bug." What is the most accurate explanation and fix?
options: The model is broken and must be replaced with a model from another vendor across the subscriptions.
The training data ends before the launch; supply current product facts with RAG or the prompt
The context window is too large, so the model ignored the product
The model has drifted, so it must be retrained from scratch every month
questions.correct_rationale: Foundation models know only what was in their training data up to a cutoff date.
questions.distractor_summary: That's expected behavior, not a bug. The practical fix is to provide current, company-specific information at query time through RAG or the prompt. Switching vendors doesn't solve it, a large context window isn't the cause, and monthly retraining from scratch is impractical.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A subscription company's churn model was accurate at launch. Over nine months, after a competitor entered the market, its predictions became steadily less reliable, even though no one changed the model. What is happening, and what's the right response?
options: Model drift; monitor performance against a baseline and retrain on recent data
Hallucination; add a content filter to the output of the model for the application.
Overfitting; delete the training data of the model throughout the organization overall.
Prompt injection; block external inputs to the model throughout the organization.
questions.correct_rationale: Model drift is performance decay as the real world moves away from the training data.
questions.distractor_summary: The response is ongoing monitoring with alert thresholds and periodic retraining. Deployed AI is never "done." Hallucination and prompt injection are generative AI issues, and overfitting shows up at launch, not gradually.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: An internal audit finds employees pasting customer contracts into free, personal generative AI websites to summarize them. What is the most effective response?
options: Ignore it, because the employees are being productive with the tools throughout the organization.
Fire the employees who pasted the customer contracts into the sites throughout the organization.
Block all AI websites for good and stop discussing the topic of AI
Provide an approved enterprise AI tool, an acceptable use policy, and data training for staff
questions.correct_rationale: This is shadow AI, and it signals real demand that the business isn't meeting.
questions.distractor_summary: Bans alone push usage further underground. The effective response channels the demand into a governed tool, sets clear rules, and teaches people why. Ignoring it risks data leakage, and punishment without alternatives damages trust.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: Agents using an internal knowledge assistant can rate answers with a thumbs up or down and type in corrections. How does this feature create business value over time?
options: It replaces the need for any governance of the AI assistant at all in this case for the company.
It creates a feedback loop showing where prompts, documents, or retrieval need work
It retrains the foundation model automatically every single night for this team as a result.
It lowers the token price that the assistant is charged each month at this stage in the near term.
questions.correct_rationale: User feedback shows where the system fails, for example missing or outdated documents or weak prompts, so the team can prioritize fixes and measure improvement.
questions.distractor_summary: It doesn't replace governance, doesn't by itself retrain a foundation model, and has no effect on pricing.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A new Chief AI Officer suspects many departments are using AI tools that haven't been approved, but no one knows which tools or what data they touch. What should come first?
options: Publish a strict policy that bans all unapproved tools immediately overall.
Buy an enterprise license for one tool and make everyone switch tomorrow
Discover and catalog the AI tools in use, their data, and their owners
Wait for a data incident to show which of the tools are risky as needed.
questions.correct_rationale: You can't govern what you can't see.
questions.distractor_summary: An AI inventory shows the actual usage, the risks, and the unmet needs, which then shape sensible policies and approved alternatives. Banning or switching tools before understanding the situation causes disruption, and waiting for an incident is negligent.

questions.domain: 1. AI Fundamentals and Literacy
questions.question: A company's marketing assistant suddenly writes noticeably different copy. The cause: the model provider released a new model version, and the application automatically switched to it. Which practice would have prevented the surprise?
options: Using a higher temperature setting for the model throughout the organization overall.
Turning off all of the monitoring of the application throughout the organization overall.
Switching to rule-based automation for the marketing copy throughout the organization.
Pinning a model version and testing new versions on test cases before adopting them
questions.correct_rationale: Version pinning plus evaluation before rollout keeps model upgrades deliberate and tested.
questions.distractor_summary: It's the generative AI version of change management. Temperature affects randomness, not versions. Removing monitoring makes things worse, and rules can't write marketing copy.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A regional bank's board asks leadership for an AI strategy. Where should the strategy start?
options: With the bank's business goals and biggest problems, then where AI can move outcomes
With a list of the newest foundation models on the market throughout the organization.
With copying the AI projects that a competitor has announced across the subscriptions.
With buying GPUs so that the bank is ready for anything
questions.correct_rationale: Good AI strategy is business strategy first: start from goals such as growth, cost, risk, or customer experience, and work back to AI opportunities.
questions.distractor_summary: Model lists, copying competitors, and buying infrastructure first are technology-led and usually produce pilots with no clear value.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A strategist is mapping AI capabilities to business outcomes for an insurance claims department. Which statement is the best capability-to-outcome mapping?
options: "We will use a large language model because it is state of the art today."
"Generative AI will transform everything in our whole organization soon."
"Summarization will cut adjuster reading time per claim, lowering cost and speeding settlement."
"We will deploy agents in every one of the departments by the third quarter."
questions.correct_rationale: A strong mapping traces the chain from capability (summarization) to an operational effect (less reading time) to measurable business outcomes (cost per claim, cycle time).
questions.distractor_summary: The other statements name technology or ambition without a measurable outcome.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A 300-person logistics firm has no data scientists and a modest IT budget. It wants to use AI to reduce invoice processing time and improve customer email response. Which strategic approach best fits its resources?
options: Hire a 15-person ML research team to build proprietary models throughout the organization overall.
Train its own foundation model to create a competitive moat throughout the organization overall.
Postpone AI until the firm can afford a data science team throughout the organization overall.
Favor managed AI services and ready-made solutions, building only where it differentiates
questions.correct_rationale: Strategy must fit available resources.
questions.distractor_summary: Invoice extraction and email assistance are common needs that managed services and SaaS handle well, with fast time to value and no ML team. Building research teams or foundation models doesn't fit the firm's scale, and waiting gives up achievable value.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A retailer's AI steering committee has approved eight initiatives. All eight are multi-year, high-risk transformation bets, and none are expected to show results within 12 months. What is the main strategic concern?
options: The portfolio lacks quick wins that build momentum, prove value, and keep sponsors
There are too few initiatives in the portfolio of the retailer across the subscriptions.
High-risk bets should never be funded by any company throughout the organization overall.
Results within 12 months are impossible with AI for retail across the subscriptions.
questions.correct_rationale: A healthy AI portfolio balances quick wins, which show early value and build skills and credibility, with strategic bets for long-term advantage.
questions.distractor_summary: An all-bets portfolio risks losing executive support before anything pays off. Strategic bets are fine in moderation, and many AI uses deliver value quickly.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: Procurement approvals at a manufacturer take 15 days. Analysis shows each request passes through five sequential sign-offs, three of which duplicate checks already done. A vendor proposes an AI agent to "speed up approvals." What should the strategist recommend first?
options: Deploy the AI agent across all five of the sign-offs throughout the organization overall.
Redesign the process to remove redundant steps, then see if AI adds value to the rest
Fine-tune a model on the past approval emails of the firm throughout the organization overall.
Add a sixth AI review step to improve the quality of the checks across the subscriptions.
questions.correct_rationale: Automating a broken process just makes waste faster.
questions.distractor_summary: The root cause is process design, not missing intelligence. Recognizing when AI isn't the (first) answer is an explicit exam theme. After simplifying the process, AI may still help, for example by pre-checking requests.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A hospital wants to reduce nurses' documentation burden. One option is to have AI write and file nursing notes with no human review. Another is to have AI draft the notes for nurses to review and sign. Which is the stronger strategic choice, and why?
options: Full automation, because it saves the most time in theory
Neither option, because healthcare can't use AI for notes
AI drafts with nurse review: most of the savings and clinical accountability remain
Full automation, because the nurses will resist any change anyway
questions.correct_rationale: In high-stakes settings, augmenting people (AI drafts, a human decides) usually gives the best balance of value, safety, accountability, and adoption.
questions.distractor_summary: Full automation of clinical records raises patient-safety and liability risk. Healthcare uses AI widely, and assuming resistance isn't a strategy.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: Which element is most essential to include when an AI initiative is approved as part of the strategy?
options: The name of the foundation model that the team will use for the work at this stage.
The vendor's marketing materials that describe the product features in the near term.
A guarantee of 100% accuracy that the vendor puts in writing
A measurable outcome with KPIs, a baseline, and an accountable business owner
questions.correct_rationale: Without a defined outcome, a baseline, KPIs, and an owner, you can't judge success or decide whether to scale or stop.
questions.distractor_summary: Model choice is a later technical decision, vendor materials aren't a plan, and no AI system can promise 100% accuracy.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A company debates who should own its AI strategy. The CIO wants IT to own it, and business unit heads want to run their own AI plans independently. Which ownership model is most effective?
options: Joint ownership: business leaders own outcomes, with tech, data, and risk partners
IT alone should own it, because AI is a technology matter
Each business unit alone should own it, with no coordination between the other units
The AI vendor should own it, because it knows the technology best
questions.correct_rationale: AI value is realized in business processes, but it depends on shared platforms, data, security, and governance.
questions.distractor_summary: Effective strategy is co-owned and sponsored at the executive level. IT alone loses business focus, uncoordinated units duplicate effort and risk, and outsourcing the strategy to a vendor creates conflicts of interest.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A company wrote a detailed three-year AI strategy two years ago and hasn't revisited it. Since then, model capabilities have improved dramatically, prices have dropped, and two of its planned custom builds are now available as low-cost managed services. What does this situation show?
options: Strategies should never be written down by a company throughout the organization by default.
The original strategy was correct and must be followed to the end throughout the organization.
AI strategy is a living plan, reviewed regularly so that priorities and investments adjust
The company should stop using AI until the market stabilizes throughout the organization overall.
questions.correct_rationale: The AI landscape moves fast, so strategy needs regular reviews (for example quarterly) to reprioritize, switch builds to buys, and reallocate funding.
questions.distractor_summary: Following an outdated plan wastes money, and pausing gives up value. Writing a strategy down is fine; the mistake is never updating it.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A distributor is picking its first generative AI pilot. Option 1 is AI-driven dynamic pricing: very high potential value, but pricing data is scattered across five systems and needs a year of cleanup. Option 2 is AI drafting answers to sales-rep product questions from an existing, well-maintained product catalog: moderate value, data ready, low risk. Which should be the first pilot?
options: Option 1, because the highest possible value always goes first
Option 2, because it pairs solid value with high feasibility and low risk
Neither option, until every piece of the company's data is perfect in the near term.
Both options at once, with an equal amount of funding for each
questions.correct_rationale: Use-case evaluation weighs value against feasibility (especially data readiness), risk, and time to value.
questions.distractor_summary: A feasible, moderate-value pilot builds capability and credibility. The pricing initiative can start its data foundation work in parallel. Waiting for perfect data stalls progress, and splitting focus raises risk.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: An HR team proposes AI to automatically screen out job applicants. The projected time savings are large. How should this use case be evaluated compared with an AI tool that drafts job descriptions?
options: Identically to the other case, since both are HR use cases of the company
Approve the screening tool first, because it saves the most time
Reject both of the proposals, because HR data is sensitive by nature
Treat screening as higher risk: require bias testing, explainability, and human review
questions.correct_rationale: Use-case evaluation must weigh risk, not just value.
questions.distractor_summary: Automated decisions about people's employment are high-risk, and regulations such as the EU AI Act classify them that way, so they need much stronger controls. Drafting job descriptions is lower risk, with a person reviewing the output. Rejecting all HR AI is overly cautious.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A transformation office plots candidate AI use cases on a value-versus-feasibility matrix. Which quadrant holds the "quick wins" to pursue first?
options: High value and high feasibility
High value and low feasibility in practice.
Low value and high feasibility
Low value and low feasibility
questions.correct_rationale: Quick wins deliver meaningful value and are easy to execute because data, skills, and integration are ready.
questions.distractor_summary: High-value, low-feasibility items are strategic bets that need deliberate investment. Low-value, high-feasibility items are "maybe later." Low-value, low-feasibility items should be dropped.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A two-week proof of concept shows that a generative AI model can draft accurate responses to warranty claims using the company's data. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Roll out to all 2,000 service agents next Monday throughout the organization for the team.
Run a pilot with a limited group of real users, measuring agreed KPIs against a baseline
Declare success and close the project right away throughout the organization for the team.
Start a second proof of concept with a different model throughout the organization overall.
questions.correct_rationale: A proof of concept proves technical feasibility ("can it work?").
questions.distractor_summary: A pilot proves business value and adoption ("does it deliver results with real users?"). Jumping straight to full rollout skips that test. Stopping after the proof of concept captures no value, and another proof of concept delays learning.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: Before launching a 90-day pilot of an AI sales-forecasting tool, the sponsor asks how the team will decide whether to scale it. What should be agreed before the pilot starts?
options: Nothing; the team will decide on how the users feel at the end of it
The model that the vendor will be using for the tool in two years
Measurable success criteria, thresholds to scale, iterate, or stop, and a baseline
A promise that the pilot will be scaled no matter what happens
questions.correct_rationale: Criteria agreed in advance, such as a forecast error reduction of at least X% or a weekly adoption rate of at least Y%, prevent goalposts from moving and allow objective stage-gate decisions.
questions.distractor_summary: Gut feel invites bias, future model plans are irrelevant, and guaranteeing a scale-up defeats the purpose of a pilot.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A pilot has run for six months and gone through two rounds of improvements. Adoption is still 12%, against a target of 60%, and measured savings are a fraction of the business case. The team argues for more funding because "we've already spent $400,000." What should the steering committee do?
options: Approve more funding, because stopping would waste the $400,000 already spent
Scale it company-wide in the hope that the adoption will increase
Keep running it indefinitely without any new targets or deadlines
Stop it, capture the lessons, and reallocate the funds to stronger use cases
questions.correct_rationale: Money already spent shouldn't drive future decisions; that's the sunk cost fallacy.
questions.distractor_summary: When a pilot repeatedly misses its pre-agreed criteria, a disciplined portfolio stops it and moves the funds. Scaling a failing pilot spreads the failure, and running it with no targets is how "pilot purgatory" happens.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A pilot of AI-assisted patient triage is meeting all its quality and value targets. However, the national regulator has announced new guidance for AI in triage, due in four months, and the requirements aren't yet known. What is the most sensible portfolio decision?
options: Terminate the initiative permanently and archive the work across the subscriptions.
Scale nationwide immediately, before the new rules arrive across the subscriptions.
Pause scaling, keep the pilot's learnings, and resume once the guidance is clear
Ignore the regulator, because the pilot is working well throughout the organization.
questions.correct_rationale: Portfolio decisions include scale, iterate, *pause*, and stop.
questions.distractor_summary: Pausing fits when the use case works but an external factor, here regulatory uncertainty, makes scaling risky right now. Terminating throws away proven value, and rushing ahead or ignoring the regulator creates compliance risk.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A pilot of an AI writing assistant for the support team met every success criterion: 70% weekly adoption, 25% faster resolution, and satisfaction scores holding steady. What should come next?
options: Scale in phases to more teams, with monitoring, training, and support in place
Stop the initiative, because pilots are only experiments and never real products
Start over with a new proof of concept for the support team
Remove the success metrics now that the pilot has finished
questions.correct_rationale: Meeting criteria agreed in advance triggers the decision to scale.
questions.distractor_summary: Phased scaling, with monitoring and change support, manages risk while capturing value. Stopping or restarting wastes proven results, and metrics should continue into production to confirm the value holds.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: Which is the best-defined AI use case statement?
options: "Use AI in finance, so that the whole department becomes more modern this year." in practice in this case.
"Help payables clerks extract invoice data, cutting handling time from 9 to 3 minutes in six months."
"Deploy the most advanced model that is available on the market this year."
"Make operations smarter with generative AI, in every one of the departments." for the company at this stage.
questions.correct_rationale: A good use case names the users, the problem, and a measurable outcome with a baseline, a target, and a timeframe.
questions.distractor_summary: The other statements are vague ambitions or technology choices with no way to measure success.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: Over two years, a company has launched 14 AI pilots. Each impressed at demo day, but none reached production. Interviews show the pilots had no named business owners, no agreed success criteria, and no budget or plan for production. What best describes the problem and the fix?
options: Model quality; switch to a larger foundation model for the next round for this team as a result.
Too few pilots; launch 20 more pilots in the next year over time in practice in this case.
The technology isn't ready; wait another two years before trying again in the near term.
Pilot purgatory; require an owner, success criteria, and a funded path to production
questions.correct_rationale: Pilot purgatory comes from weak governance and planning, not weak technology.
questions.distractor_summary: Fixing the approval process, with an owner, criteria, and a scale plan up front, turns experiments into value. Bigger models and more pilots repeat the pattern, and the evidence shows the technology works at demo level.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A company ranks AI use cases with a weighted scorecard covering value, feasibility, strategic fit, and risk. A proposal to use AI to set individual insurance premiums automatically, with no human review, scores highest overall. But the legal team rates its compliance risk as "unacceptable" under current regulations. What should happen?
options: Approve it, because it has the highest total score on the scorecard
Average the legal concern into the score and proceed if it still ranks first
Don't approve it as is; treat unacceptable risk as a gate and redesign it with human review
Hide the legal rating from the steering committee, to keep the ranking simple for the company.
questions.correct_rationale: Some criteria act as gates rather than weights.
questions.distractor_summary: Unacceptable legal or ethical risk stops a use case no matter how valuable it is. Redesigning it with human oversight, explainability, and compliant data use may bring it within risk tolerance. Averaging the risk away or hiding the rating undermines governance.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A specialty insurer has 30 years of proprietary claims and underwriting data. Its pricing accuracy is its main competitive advantage, and it has an experienced data science team. It wants AI to improve risk pricing. Which approach fits best?
options: Build a custom solution on a managed ML platform using its proprietary data
Buy the same off-the-shelf pricing tool that its competitors use for the team.
Avoid AI to protect its data from exposure throughout the organization overall.
Let a vendor own both the pricing model and the data across the subscriptions.
questions.correct_rationale: Build when the capability is a core differentiator, the company has unique data, and it has the skills.
questions.distractor_summary: A managed platform such as Amazon SageMaker AI reduces the infrastructure burden. Buying the competitors' tool erases the advantage, avoiding AI gives up value, and handing over the model and data loses control of the core asset.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A regional retailer wants a generative AI shopping assistant in production within four months for the holiday season. It has strong product data but no in-house AI experience, and hiring would take six months. What's the best approach?
options: Wait until the hiring of the new technical team is complete first in this case for the company.
Build it with the existing web team, who would learn as they go
Cancel the initiative for this holiday season and revisit it next year over time in practice.
Partner with an experienced AWS Partner, with knowledge transfer to build skills
questions.correct_rationale: Partnering fills skill gaps and speeds delivery when the timeline is tight.
questions.distractor_summary: Building knowledge transfer into the engagement reduces long-term dependence on the partner. Waiting misses the season, learning on the job risks quality and timing, and cancelling gives up a viable opportunity.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A legal-services firm wants a research assistant grounded in its proprietary case library. It doesn't want to train its own models but does want to control its data and workflow. Which approach best describes this?
options: Pure buy: use a generic consumer chatbot for the research of the firm
Pure build: train its own large language model on the case library
Hybrid: managed models (such as Amazon Bedrock) plus its own retrieval layer
Pure partner: outsource all of the legal research to an outside vendor at this stage.
questions.correct_rationale: The hybrid approach is common: buy or rent the commodity layer (foundation models) and build the differentiating layer (proprietary data, RAG, workflow, user experience).
questions.distractor_summary: A consumer chatbot lacks control and grounding, training a model from scratch is wasteful, and outsourcing everything gives away the firm's differentiator.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: Option 1, building in-house, has an estimated development cost of $150,000. Option 2, a SaaS subscription, costs $90,000 a year. The CFO is leaning toward building because "$150,000 once is cheaper than $90,000 every year." What should the analysis compare?
options: Only the upfront price tags of the two options in the table
Total cost of ownership over the lifetime: hosting, maintenance, staff, and upgrades
Only the discount that the vendor has offered to the company at this stage in the near term.
Which of the two options sounds more innovative to the board for this team as a result.
questions.correct_rationale: Build costs continue well after launch: infrastructure, maintenance engineers, model updates, security, and monitoring.
questions.distractor_summary: Comparing total cost of ownership, plus time to value, gives a fair answer. Sticker prices, discounts alone, and how innovative an option sounds lead to poor decisions.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A company is concerned that committing to a single model provider will leave it stuck if better or cheaper models appear. Which strategy best reduces this lock-in risk?
options: Sign a 10-year exclusive contract with one provider for the best discount in every region.
Avoid all generative AI until the market consolidates throughout the organization overall.
Build every model in-house to avoid having any vendors throughout the organization overall.
Use a platform with a choice of models, and keep data, prompts, and evaluations portable
questions.correct_rationale: A multi-model platform, which is how Amazon Bedrock is positioned, plus portable assets lets the company switch models as the market changes.
questions.distractor_summary: Long exclusive contracts increase lock-in, waiting gives up value, and building everything in-house is costly and creates a different kind of dependency.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A bank learns that a competitor will launch an AI-powered mortgage pre-approval experience in three months. Building a comparable solution internally would take 12 months. A proven vendor solution can be integrated in about 10 weeks and meets the bank's compliance requirements. Which factor most favors buying here?
options: Buying is always cheaper than building for the bank
Vendors never have security issues in their products across the subscriptions.
Time to value: buying lets the bank answer the competitive threat in time
Building would give the bank more control over everything for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: When speed matters competitively and a compliant solution exists, time to value can decide build vs.
questions.distractor_summary: buy. Buying isn't always cheaper, vendors do carry risks that need due diligence, and while building offers control, that argues *for* building, not buying.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A European healthcare provider wants a clinical documentation assistant. The leading SaaS product can't guarantee that patient data stays within the EU, which the provider's data residency rules require. The provider has a small cloud team but no ML researchers. What's the best approach?
options: Buy the SaaS anyway and accept the compliance gap for patient data
Build on a managed model platform in an EU AWS Region, with no model training
Train a proprietary clinical foundation model from scratch in the EU
Abandon the initiative entirely and drop the whole clinical documentation project
questions.correct_rationale: Constraints shape the decision.
questions.distractor_summary: Data residency rules out the SaaS product, and a lack of ML researchers rules out training a model. A hybrid build on managed services in a compliant Region meets residency needs with a small team, and a partner can speed delivery. Accepting the gap creates regulatory exposure, and abandoning the initiative gives up the value.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A support director plans to launch an AI assistant next month and prove its value to finance six months later. What must the team do *before* launch?
options: Measure the baseline now: average handle time, cost per contact, and satisfaction
Choose the colors of the dashboard that the finance team will see
Nothing at all, since the savings will be obvious afterward
Ask the vendor to provide the ROI figure that the finance team wants to see afterward
questions.correct_rationale: You can't prove improvement without a "before" measurement.
questions.distractor_summary: A baseline taken before launch is the anchor for every KPI and ROI claim. Waiting until afterward loses the comparison, and an ROI figure from the vendor isn't independent evidence.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: Three months into a sales-copilot rollout, revenue impact can't be measured yet. Which metric is the best *leading* indicator that the initiative is on track?
options: Annual revenue growth of the whole company across the subscriptions.
End-of-year profit margin of the business unit for the application.
Weekly active usage of the copilot among the target sales reps
Three-year customer lifetime value of the accounts for the team.
questions.correct_rationale: Leading indicators, such as adoption, usage, and user satisfaction, give early signals.
questions.distractor_summary: If people don't use the tool, no value will follow. Revenue, margin, and lifetime value are lagging indicators that show results only after months or years.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: An AI tool saves each of 100 claims processors about 90 minutes a day. The business case counts this as "$2 million in annual savings." Headcount, overtime, and work volume all stay the same. What's the main problem with this claim?
options: The time saved is miscalculated by the team that wrote the business case
AI can't save time for the claims processors at all, in any form
The savings should be doubled to include the overtime that the company saves each year
Freed time is a soft saving; it is value only if redeployed or if overtime falls
questions.correct_rationale: Hard savings reduce cash spending.
questions.distractor_summary: Soft savings free up capacity. If nothing changes in output, cost, or quality, the freed time produces no measurable value. Strong business cases say how the capacity will be redeployed and track that outcome.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: Online sales rose 8% in the month an AI product-recommendation engine launched. The same month also had a holiday promotion and a competitor's outage. How can the team best attribute the lift to the AI?
options: Credit all 8% to the AI, since it launched in the same month
Run an A/B test: compare a random group seeing AI recommendations with a control group
Ask customers whether they noticed the AI recommendations when they shopped for the company.
Credit none of it to the AI, since the attribution is impossible
questions.correct_rationale: Control groups separate the AI's effect from other factors, such as promotions, seasonality, and competitor events.
questions.distractor_summary: Crediting all of the lift to the AI is false attribution, customer surveys can't measure the causal impact, and attribution is very possible with good experiment design.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A data science team reports to the executive committee that the new fraud model's F1 score improved from 0.71 to 0.84. Executives ask, "So what?" Which KPI would communicate value best?
options: Precision and recall reported to four decimal places throughout the organization overall.
The number of parameters in the model throughout the organization for the application.
Fraud losses avoided each month and fewer legitimate transactions wrongly declined
Training time in GPU hours throughout the organization across the subscriptions overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Executives need business KPIs: money saved, customer friction reduced, risk lowered.
questions.distractor_summary: Model metrics like F1, precision, and recall matter to technical teams but should be translated into business outcomes. Parameter counts and training time say nothing about value.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A startup is piloting a generative AI feature. It has no idea whether usage will be 1,000 or 100,000 requests a month. Which pricing approach best fits this stage?
options: A multi-year capacity commitment for the generative AI feature in the near term.
Buying dedicated GPUs upfront for the generative AI feature for this team.
Seat-based licenses for every possible user of the feature
Consumption-based (on-demand) pricing, paying per token or per request
questions.correct_rationale: When demand is uncertain or variable, pay-as-you-go pricing avoids paying for idle capacity and scales with real usage.
questions.distractor_summary: Commitments, dedicated hardware, and per-seat licenses all assume demand you can't yet predict.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A large insurer's generative AI claims assistant now handles a steady, predictable, high volume of requests around the clock. Performance must be consistent at peak times. Which Amazon Bedrock pricing option fits best?
options: Provisioned Throughput, which reserves dedicated model capacity for a term
On-demand pricing only, with no reserved capacity for the steady volume of requests
Batch inference, which processes requests in bulk at a lower price
A free tier, which is meant for early experiments and small tests only
questions.correct_rationale: Provisioned Throughput reserves model capacity, giving consistent performance for steady, high-volume production, and longer commitments lower the hourly rate.
questions.distractor_summary: On-demand suits variable workloads. Batch suits non-urgent bulk jobs, not real-time assistance, and a free tier isn't a production option.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: Each night, a bank needs to summarize 200,000 archived documents for a compliance review. Results are needed by the next morning, not in real time. Which approach most reduces cost?
options: Real-time on-demand calls, one document at a time through the endpoint over time in practice.
Batch inference, which processes requests in bulk at a lower price for supported models
The largest available model for every single one of the documents
A higher temperature setting for the compliance summaries of the bank
questions.correct_rationale: For large jobs that aren't urgent, batch inference is far cheaper.
questions.distractor_summary: On Amazon Bedrock it's priced well below on-demand for supported models. Real-time calls cost more without any benefit here, the largest model raises cost, and temperature has no effect on price.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A retailer uses the largest, most capable foundation model to classify customer emails into five categories. An evaluation shows a much smaller model reaches the same accuracy on this task at a fraction of the cost per request. What should the retailer do?
options: Keep the largest model, because a bigger model is always safer for the application.
Use both of the models on every one of the emails throughout the organization overall.
Right-size: switch this task to the smaller model, and keep monitoring quality
Stop classifying the emails of the customers altogether across the subscriptions.
questions.correct_rationale: Choosing the smallest model that meets the quality bar is one of the biggest generative AI cost levers.
questions.distractor_summary: Simple tasks rarely need the most powerful model. Running both models doubles cost, and dropping the task gives up its value.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: After launch, a CFO wants to see actual month-by-month AWS spending on the company's generative AI projects, with trends and breakdowns by project. Which tool fits best?
options: AWS Pricing Calculator, which estimates the cost of planned workloads
AWS Marketplace, where the company buys third-party software overall.
Amazon SageMaker AI, which builds and trains ML models
AWS Cost Explorer, with cost allocation tags for each project
questions.correct_rationale: Cost Explorer analyzes *actual* spending and trends, and tags let costs be broken down by project.
questions.distractor_summary: The Pricing Calculator estimates costs *before* building, Marketplace is for buying third-party software, and SageMaker AI is an ML platform.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A vendor's sales deck promises "40% productivity gains" from its AI writing tool, based on studies at other companies. The CFO wants to use 40% in the investment case. What's the most sound approach?
options: Run a measured pilot against the company's own baseline and use the observed results
Use 40% in the business case, since the vendor's studies are published and reviewed
Double the figure to 80% in order to look more ambitious to finance
Use 0%, because the claims of a vendor are always false
questions.correct_rationale: Results depend on context: workflows, users, data, and adoption.
questions.distractor_summary: A pilot measured against your own baseline gives credible figures, and conservative assumptions protect the business case. Adopting, inflating, or dismissing the vendor's figure without evidence are all weak practice.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: Every competitor in an industry can access the same leading foundation models through cloud platforms. Where is a company's *durable* AI competitive advantage most likely to come from?
options: Being the only company that uses a specific public model throughout the organization in every region.
Proprietary data, deep workflow integration, and customer experience that rivals can't copy easily
Spending the most money on the fees for model usage throughout the organization for the application.
Announcing its AI projects before its competitors do throughout the organization for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: Foundation models are increasingly a commodity anyone can rent.
questions.distractor_summary: Advantage comes from what others can't replicate: unique data (a "data moat"), processes redesigned around AI, and a better customer experience. Exclusive model access is rare and short-lived, and spending or announcements don't create an edge.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: An online retailer uses AI to tailor homepage products and email offers to each shopper's browsing and purchase history. Conversion rates rise 12%. Which type of AI value does this mainly represent?
options: Operational efficiency, through fewer manual steps in the process
Regulatory compliance, through better records of the activities
Better customer experience and revenue through personalization
Infrastructure cost reduction, through less spending on the cloud
questions.correct_rationale: Personalization improves relevance for customers and drives revenue through higher conversion.
questions.distractor_summary: Operational efficiency would mean cutting cost or time in internal processes. Compliance and infrastructure cost aren't what this example delivers.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: An agricultural-equipment maker starts selling farmers a subscription service that uses AI on sensor data from their machines to predict crop yields and recommend planting schedules. Which kind of AI value does this represent?
options: Back-office cost reduction, through fewer manual tasks for the staff over time.
Employee productivity, through faster work by the staff of the maker
Data cleanup, through better quality of the sensor records
Business model innovation: a new revenue stream built on AI and data
questions.correct_rationale: Moving from one-time equipment sales to an AI-powered recurring service changes how the company makes money.
questions.distractor_summary: That's business model innovation, the highest-value and highest-uncertainty kind of AI transformation. The other options describe internal improvements.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A mid-market manufacturer is deciding whether to be first in its industry to deploy AI-generated supplier contract summaries, a useful but non-core back-office capability. Proven solutions are emerging fast. What's the most sensible stance?
options: Fast follower: adopt proven tools once they mature, and save effort for what differentiates
First mover at any cost, building a custom solution for the summaries right now at this stage.
Never adopt it, because back-office AI has no value to a manufacturer
Wait ten years until the technology reaches full maturity for everyone in the near term for this team.
questions.correct_rationale: For non-core capabilities, being a fast follower lowers risk and cost while still capturing value.
questions.distractor_summary: Being first matters most where the capability is a real differentiator. Refusing or waiting a decade gives up clear efficiency gains.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A bank added a generative AI assistant to its loan-processing workflow, but the 11-step process, handoffs, and approval rules stayed exactly the same. Loan cycle time improved only 3%. What best explains the limited impact?
options: The foundation model is too small to handle the loan documents well
AI value depends on redesigning the process; an unchanged workflow limits the gains
Generative AI can't help with any of the work in a bank
The assistant needs a higher temperature setting to handle the loans of the bank
questions.correct_rationale: Transformational value usually comes from rethinking the workflow: removing steps, changing handoffs, and moving people to exception handling.
questions.distractor_summary: AI layered onto a legacy process inherits its bottlenecks. Model size and temperature aren't the limiting factors, and banking has many proven AI uses.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A retail chain's regional managers set inventory levels by gut feel. Leadership deploys an AI tool that shows demand forecasts, what-if scenarios, and recommended stock levels, while managers still make the final call. How does AI create value here?
options: By replacing all of the regional managers of the chain across the subscriptions.
By eliminating the need to hold any inventory in stores across the subscriptions.
By improving the quality and speed of human decisions with better information
By lowering the cloud costs of the retail chain throughout the organization overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Better decision-making is a core AI value lever.
questions.distractor_summary: AI provides forecasts and scenarios, and people apply judgment and accountability. The managers stay in place, inventory still matters, and cloud cost isn't the point.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A competitor announces a flashy AI avatar for its mobile app. The CEO asks the team to "build the same thing by next quarter." What's the strategist's best response?
options: Build an identical avatar immediately, to keep up with the competitor in practice.
Ignore all of the competitor's moves for good and never respond
Copy the competitor's entire AI roadmap over the course of a year
Check real customer needs and strategy fit, then follow, differentiate, or skip
questions.correct_rationale: Competitive moves should be weighed against your own customers' needs, your strategy, and the evidence of value.
questions.distractor_summary: Reflexive copying wastes money on features that may not matter. Ignoring competitors forever is complacent, and copying a whole roadmap gives up your own direction.

questions.domain: 2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
questions.question: A software company's AI self-service assistant resolves most customer issues. That reduces demand for its paid "premium support" tier, a meaningful revenue line. How should leadership evaluate the initiative?
options: Cancel the assistant to protect the revenue of the premium support tier
Assess the net impact: lost support revenue against better satisfaction, retention, and costs
Hide the assistant from the premium customers of the company
Raise the prices of the premium support tier to compensate for it
questions.correct_rationale: AI can cannibalize existing revenue.
questions.distractor_summary: Strategic evaluation looks at the whole picture, because if the company doesn't offer a better experience, a competitor will. Cancelling or hiding the assistant protects short-term revenue at long-term cost, and price hikes ignore the change in what customers value.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: A logistics company insists that operators must be able to override its AI dispatch system's decisions and shut it down immediately if it misbehaves. Which responsible AI dimension does this requirement address?
options: Fairness, which means similar treatment of similar groups
Explainability, which means the reasons for a decision are clear overall.
Controllability, which means humans can override or stop the system
Veracity, which means the outputs are true and correct
questions.correct_rationale: Controllability is the ability to monitor and steer AI behavior, including overrides, fallbacks, and kill switches.
questions.distractor_summary: Fairness concerns equal treatment, explainability concerns understanding outputs, and veracity concerns correctness.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: An insurance chatbot works well in testing. In production, it gives wrong answers when customers make typos, use slang, or ask unusual multi-part questions. Which responsible AI dimension needs strengthening?
options: Transparency, which means being open about how the system works for the application.
Veracity and robustness, which means correct, reliable behavior on messy inputs
Fairness, which means similar treatment of similar groups across the subscriptions.
Governance, which means the policies and oversight of the system in every region.
questions.correct_rationale: Veracity and robustness mean producing correct outputs even with unexpected, noisy, or adversarial inputs.
questions.distractor_summary: Testing should cover realistic edge cases, not just clean examples. The other dimensions don't address reliability under messy real-world inputs.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: A marketing team wants to send full customer records, including names, addresses, birth dates, and purchase histories, to a generative AI model to write campaign copy. The copy only needs general segment preferences. What responsible AI practice applies?
options: Data minimization: send only the data that the task needs, and mask personal details
Send everything, since more data always improves the output of a model in practice in this case.
Send the data to as many models as possible and compare the results
Skip the campaign entirely and drop the project for the marketing team for the company.
questions.correct_rationale: Privacy and security include using only the minimum data needed.
questions.distractor_summary: Segment-level preferences meet the need without exposing personal details. More data isn't always better, spreading data across many models increases exposure, and cancelling the campaign is unnecessary.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: For a regulated small-business lending decision, the data science team presents two models. One is a complex model with 2% higher accuracy but limited interpretability. The other is an interpretable model whose decision factors can be clearly explained. Regulators require specific reasons for every decline. Which choice best reflects responsible AI leadership?
options: The complex model, because the accuracy of a model always wins in the end at this stage.
Deploy both of the models and let the customers choose between them for this team as a result.
The interpretable model, accepting a small accuracy cost to meet explainability rules
Neither model, so the lender stops lending to small businesses altogether in the near term.
questions.correct_rationale: Responsible AI often means weighing trade-offs openly, such as accuracy against explainability.
questions.distractor_summary: When regulation and fairness require explanations, a small accuracy gain doesn't justify losing them. Documenting the trade-off is part of governance. Letting customers choose models makes no sense, and abandoning the market is unnecessary.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: A project team says responsible AI was "handled" because an ethics committee approved the project once, at kickoff. What's wrong with this view?
options: Ethics committees should never review any of the AI projects of a company
Responsible AI spans the whole lifecycle, because risks change as data and models change
Responsible AI only matters after a public incident has happened
Nothing is wrong, because one approval at the start is enough
questions.correct_rationale: Risks such as drift, emerging bias, and new misuse patterns appear after launch.
questions.distractor_summary: Responsible AI is a continuous lifecycle practice, not a single checkpoint. Committee review is useful but not enough on its own, and waiting for an incident is reactive.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: On a previous AI project, legal and security reviewed the solution only one week before launch. They found serious issues, and the launch slipped four months. What practice would prevent this next time?
options: Skip the legal and security reviews to protect the timelines for the application.
Have legal and security review the solution only after the launch in every region.
Governance by design: involve legal, security, risk, and privacy from the start
Hire more developers so that the team can move faster throughout the organization.
questions.correct_rationale: Building governance in from the start catches issues when they're cheap to fix, and it often speeds delivery overall.
questions.distractor_summary: Skipping reviews or postponing them until after launch shifts risk into production, and adding developers doesn't fix late-stage compliance gaps.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: A company is forming an AI governance council to approve and oversee AI initiatives. Which membership is most effective?
options: Cross-functional: business, legal, compliance, risk, security, data, technology, and HR
Only the data science team of the company, who build the models
Only the legal department of the company, who handle the contracts
Only external vendors that supply the AI tools to the company
questions.correct_rationale: AI risks and value span many functions: legal, ethical, security, data, people, and business outcomes.
questions.distractor_summary: Cross-functional governance brings all those views together. A single-function council has blind spots, and vendors have conflicts of interest.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: Why should an organization maintain an AI inventory, also called an AI registry?
options: To count how many GPUs the organization owns in its data centers as a result over time.
To list the favorite AI websites of the employees of the company in practice in this case.
To replace the need for any AI policy at all in the company
To keep a central record of each AI system: owner, purpose, data, risk, and status
questions.correct_rationale: You can't govern what you can't see.
questions.distractor_summary: An AI inventory shows what exists, who owns it, what data it touches, and how risky it is, and it helps uncover shadow AI. It isn't a hardware count or a list of favorite sites, and it supports policy rather than replacing it.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: A business team wants to understand a model's intended uses, limitations, performance characteristics, and responsible AI considerations before adopting it. Which documentation is designed for this?
options: An invoice from the vendor of the model throughout the organization.
A model card (AWS publishes AI Service Cards for its AI services)
A marketing brochure from the vendor of the model for the application.
A source-code repository for the model throughout the organization.
questions.correct_rationale: Model cards and AWS AI Service Cards document intended use, limitations, performance, and responsible AI design, which supports transparency and informed adoption.
questions.distractor_summary: Invoices and brochures don't cover this, and source code isn't written for business readers.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: An AI system wrongly denies a batch of legitimate warranty claims. In the post-incident review, the business, data science, and vendor teams each say "the AI made the decision." What governance gap does this reveal?
options: The model needs more parameters to make fewer mistakes in the future
The vendor should be solely responsible for the outcomes of the system for this team.
No clearly named accountable owner existed for the outcomes of the AI system
AI decisions can never be audited by anyone at the company
questions.correct_rationale: Accountability must rest with people.
questions.distractor_summary: Every AI system needs a named business owner who is accountable for its outcomes, supported by clear roles (for example, a RACI chart). "The AI did it" is never acceptable. Model size is irrelevant, vendors share but don't absorb accountability, and AI decisions can be audited with proper logging.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: A regulator asks a bank to show exactly how its AI system reached a specific loan decision 18 months ago. Which governance capability makes this possible?
options: An audit trail logging inputs, model version, output, human review, and approvals
A newer model version that gives better answers than the old one
The vendor's marketing materials about the model of the bank
The recollection of the employees who were involved in the decision
questions.correct_rationale: Audit trails, together with model versioning, let organizations reconstruct and justify past AI decisions, which is essential for regulated use.
questions.distractor_summary: A newer model can't explain an old decision, and marketing materials and memories aren't evidence.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: An internal review finds that a pricing model "replaced" two years ago is still quietly running inside an old reporting app. It's making outdated recommendations that some managers still use. Which governance gap does this reveal?
options: Too much documentation of the AI systems that the company runs
Models that are too small for the workloads that the company has
Excessive human oversight of the AI systems of the company
Governance that doesn't cover the full lifecycle, including formal retirement of AI systems
questions.correct_rationale: Lifecycle governance runs from idea to retirement.
questions.distractor_summary: Without formal decommissioning tied to an AI inventory, old models linger and create risk. Documentation, model size, and oversight levels aren't the cause here.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: A bank applies the "three lines of defense" model to AI. Which role does the *second* line play?
options: Building and operating the AI systems day to day for the business in practice in this case.
