Independent assurance through internal audit of the controls and processes as a result over time.
Risk and compliance oversight: setting AI risk policies and challenging the first line
Selling AI products to the customers of the bank in the market
questions.correct_rationale: The first line, the business and its delivery teams, owns and manages the risk.
questions.distractor_summary: The second line, risk and compliance, sets policy and oversees it. The third line, internal audit, provides independent assurance. Sales isn't part of the model.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: Under a risk-tiered AI regulation such as the EU AI Act, which use is most likely to be classified as *high-risk* and subject to strict requirements?
options: An AI system that screens job applicants or evaluates creditworthiness
A spam filter for the internal email of a company across the subscriptions.
An AI that suggests songs for a playlist throughout the organization overall.
A grammar checker for marketing drafts of a company for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: Risk-tiered regulation puts AI that affects people's access to jobs, credit, education, or essential services in the high-risk category.
questions.distractor_summary: Those uses require risk management, data governance, documentation, human oversight, and transparency. The other examples are minimal-risk uses.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: A multinational's legal team distinguishes "data residency" from "data sovereignty" when planning an AI deployment. Which statement is correct?
options: They mean the same thing in the plans of a multinational company
Residency is about which country's laws apply; sovereignty is about where data is stored in practice.
Residency is about where data is stored; sovereignty is about which country's laws govern it
Neither concept applies to AI workloads of a multinational company
questions.correct_rationale: Residency is about physical location, for example choosing an AWS Region.
questions.distractor_summary: Sovereignty is about legal jurisdiction over the data. Both shape where and how AI workloads can run. Option B reverses the definitions, and both concepts apply fully to AI.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: Which of the following is AWS's responsibility, not the customer's, when a company uses Amazon Bedrock?
options: Writing the acceptable use policy of the company for the use of AI
Securing the infrastructure and managed service that host and run the foundation models
Deciding which employees may access the customer data of the company
Reviewing the AI outputs before they are sent to the customers
questions.correct_rationale: AWS is responsible for the security *of* the cloud, including the infrastructure and managed service behind Bedrock.
questions.distractor_summary: Policies, access decisions, and reviewing outputs are the customer's responsibilities.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: A call center wants to use generative AI to summarize customer calls. The transcripts contain names, phone numbers, and account numbers that the summaries don't need. Which control best supports compliance?
options: Store the transcripts in more places for redundancy and backups
Raise the model's temperature so the summaries read more naturally
Redact or mask personal information before or during processing, for example with Bedrock Guardrails
Email the transcripts to the vendor for a manual review of the summaries
questions.correct_rationale: Redacting PII applies data minimization and lowers privacy and compliance risk.
questions.distractor_summary: Guardrails and services such as Amazon Comprehend can detect and mask sensitive information. Extra copies and emailing transcripts increase exposure, and temperature has nothing to do with privacy.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: A utility company collected customers' usage data for billing. The marketing team now wants to use the same data to train an AI model that predicts which customers will buy solar panels. What should happen first?
options: Use the data immediately, since the company already has it throughout the organization overall.
Delete all of the billing data of the customers throughout the organization for the application.
Buy external data instead, without any review throughout the organization across the subscriptions.
Ask legal and privacy if the new purpose fits the original consent, and get consent if needed
questions.correct_rationale: Privacy laws often limit data to the purposes it was collected for.
questions.distractor_summary: Reusing data for a new AI purpose may need fresh consent or a different lawful basis. Having the data doesn't mean you're allowed to use it this way, deleting billing data is extreme, and external data needs review too.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: A CISO hesitates to approve Amazon Bedrock, asking, "Will our prompts and data be used to train the foundation models or be shared with the model providers?" What's the accurate answer?
options: No. With Amazon Bedrock, prompts and outputs aren't used to train base models
Yes. All of the prompts are shared publicly with other users of the service
Yes. The model providers receive all of the prompts to improve their own models
It depends on the font that the staff use when they write the prompts for it
questions.correct_rationale: AWS states that Bedrock doesn't use customer prompts or outputs to train its base models and doesn't share them with model providers.
questions.distractor_summary: Combined with encryption and access controls, this addresses a common executive concern about enterprise generative AI. The other answers are false.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: Employees ask which company information they may use with the approved AI assistant. The company labels data as Public, Internal, Confidential, and Restricted. What's the most effective way to guide them?
options: Allow all of the data in all of the AI tools that the company has approved for this team.
Tie the AI policy to data classes, say which fit which tools, and train staff
Ban all of the data from all of the AI tools that the company has approved
Let each employee decide case by case, without any guidance from the company in the near term.
questions.correct_rationale: Linking AI use to existing data classification gives clear, scalable rules.
questions.distractor_summary: For example, Restricted data may be used only in specific approved, isolated tools. All-or-nothing rules either create risk or block value, and leaving it to each employee produces inconsistent, risky behavior.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: A European insurer wants AI to fully automate decisions on whether to pay claims, with no human involvement. Privacy regulation gives individuals rights regarding decisions based solely on automated processing that significantly affect them. What design best supports compliance?
options: Fully automate the decisions and don't tell the customers about it throughout the organization overall.
Abandon all of the AI use in claims at the insurer throughout the organization across the subscriptions.
Provide human review for significant decisions, explain the logic, and let customers contest outcomes
Move the data to another country to avoid the regulation throughout the organization for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: GDPR-style rules on automated decisions point toward human involvement, transparency about the logic, and a way for people to challenge outcomes.
questions.distractor_summary: AI can still triage and recommend. Hiding automation breaks transparency, abandoning AI gives up value, and moving data abroad doesn't remove the obligations.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: An airline's website chatbot invents a bereavement-fare refund policy. A tribunal later rules that the airline must honor what its chatbot told the customer. Which combination of controls best reduces this risk?
options: A higher temperature, for a more natural conversation with the customers
Grounding answers in approved policy documents, with citations and human escalation
Removing the chatbot's access to all of the company documents it uses
Telling customers that the answers of the chatbot are probably right
questions.correct_rationale: Hallucinations create legal and financial liability.
questions.distractor_summary: Layered controls address both the cause and the impact: grounding, citations, guardrails such as contextual grounding checks, and human escalation. Higher temperature increases fabrication, removing document access makes it worse, and a vague disclaimer won't shield the company from liability.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: A company trains a résumé-screening model on 10 years of past hiring decisions. Historically, most hires came from a narrow set of universities and backgrounds. What risk is most likely?
options: Historical bias: the model learns past patterns and unfairly disadvantages qualified candidates
Hallucination of fake résumés by the screening model of the company
Lower cloud costs for the human resources department of the company
Prompt injection by applicants who write hidden text in their résumés
questions.correct_rationale: Models learn from historical decisions, including their biases.
questions.distractor_summary: Without bias testing and correction, AI can automate past discrimination at scale. Hallucination, cost, and prompt injection aren't the main concern in this scenario.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: A marketing team uses an image-generation tool to create campaign visuals. Legal worries that some outputs may closely resemble copyrighted characters or another brand's trademarks. Which approach best manages this intellectual property risk?
options: Use any generated image, since the outputs of AI can't infringe any rights in this case.
Ban all of the generative AI use in marketing for good, in every campaign
Use approved tools with IP indemnity, plus human legal review before publishing
Add a watermark that says AI-generated and then publish every one of them
questions.correct_rationale: IP risk is managed through vendor protections, review processes, and prompt guidance.
questions.distractor_summary: AI outputs *can* infringe, a permanent ban gives up value, and a watermark discloses AI use but doesn't fix infringement.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: An attacker secretly inserts manipulated records into data that will be used to train a company's fraud model, so that certain fraudulent patterns are learned as "safe." What is this attack called?
options: Hallucination, in which the model makes up facts for the team.
Data poisoning, in which attackers corrupt the training data
Model drift, in which performance falls as the world changes overall.
Overfitting, in which a model memorizes its training data overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Data poisoning corrupts training data to manipulate model behavior.
questions.distractor_summary: Defenses include securing data pipelines, controlling access, tracking where data came from, and validating data. Hallucination, drift, and overfitting aren't deliberate attacks.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: After a year with an AI underwriting assistant, reviewers approve its recommendations 99% of the time, often within seconds and without opening the supporting documents. Several costly errors have slipped through. What risk is this?
options: Data drift, in which the input data changes over time throughout the organization.
Prompt injection, in which hidden text hijacks the model across the subscriptions.
Underfitting, in which a model is too simple to learn
Automation bias (over-reliance), where humans trust AI output without scrutiny
questions.correct_rationale: Human review only works if it's real.
questions.distractor_summary: Automation bias turns oversight into rubber-stamping. Countermeasures include training, review checklists, sampling audits, showing the AI's confidence, and periodic "challenge" cases. The other options are technical issues, not human-behavior risks.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: Users of a retailer's public shopping assistant share tricks online for getting it to ignore its rules, for example role-play prompts that make it write offensive jokes about competitors. What is this, and what's the best response?
options: Model drift; retrain the assistant every month with the newest data
Data poisoning; delete the training data of the assistant and start over
Jailbreaking; strengthen guardrails, monitor for abuse, and update defenses
Overfitting; switch the assistant to a smaller model that has fewer rules in practice.
questions.correct_rationale: Jailbreaks trick a model into bypassing its safety instructions.
questions.distractor_summary: Defense is ongoing: layered guardrails such as input and output filters and denied topics, plus abuse monitoring and regular updates. Drift, poisoning, and overfitting are different problems.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: Engineers at a manufacturer paste proprietary source code and chip designs into a free public chatbot to get debugging help. What's the primary risk?
options: Confidential data leaking outside the company's control, with a possible loss of trade secrets
Hallucinated comments in the code that the chatbot writes throughout the organization as needed.
Higher GPU costs for the company that owns the designs throughout the organization for the team.
Model drift in the chatbot over the coming months throughout the organization for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: Sending confidential IP to unapproved public tools can expose it beyond the company's control, depending on the provider's terms.
questions.distractor_summary: This is a classic shadow AI risk, and the remedy is approved enterprise tools plus policy and training. The other options aren't the main concern.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: After applying guardrails, grounding, and human review to a marketing content assistant, a small *residual* risk of occasional off-brand phrasing remains. The business considers this tolerable. What's the correct governance step?
options: Hide the residual risk from the leadership of the company
Keep adding more controls until the risk is exactly zero
Cancel the project, because some residual risk still remains
Have the accountable owner formally accept the residual risk, log it, and keep monitoring
questions.correct_rationale: Zero risk is unattainable.
questions.distractor_summary: Governance means risk is reduced to a level within tolerance, then accepted by an authorized owner, documented, and monitored. Hiding the risk breaks accountability, chasing zero wastes resources, and cancelling ignores the risk appetite.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: A company proposes an AI feature that would infer customers' health conditions from their shopping patterns to target ads. Legal and ethics reviews conclude the privacy and reputational risks can't be reduced to an acceptable level. Which risk treatment fits best?
options: Accept the risk and launch the feature quietly in the coming quarter
Avoid the risk by not building the feature; redirect effort to lower-risk personalization
Transfer the risk entirely by buying a policy of insurance for the feature as a result over time.
Mitigate it by adding a small disclaimer to the privacy policy of the company for this team.
questions.correct_rationale: When a risk can't be brought within tolerance, avoiding it, by not doing the activity, is the right treatment.
questions.distractor_summary: Accepting an intolerable risk is poor governance, insurance doesn't transfer reputational or ethical harm, and a disclaimer doesn't meaningfully reduce the harm.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: A hospital is deploying AI that suggests possible diagnoses from imaging. Which oversight model is appropriate?
options: Human-in-the-loop: a qualified clinician reviews and makes every diagnostic decision
Human-out-of-the-loop: the diagnosis of the AI goes directly to the patients in practice.
No oversight once the accuracy passes 90% in testing at the hospital
Oversight only when the patients complain about the results they receive
questions.correct_rationale: High-stakes decisions affecting health, rights, or safety need a human in the loop who decides before any action.
questions.distractor_summary: Removing humans, relying on an accuracy threshold alone, or reacting only to complaints creates unacceptable patient-safety and liability risks.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: For which use is human-out-of-the-loop automation most appropriate?
options: Approving mortgage applications for the customers of a bank
Choosing the doses of medication for the patients of a hospital
Deciding which employees to lay off during a downturn
Routing internal IT tickets to the right queue, with easy re-routing if wrong
questions.correct_rationale: Full automation fits low-risk, reversible, well-tested decisions where errors are cheap and easy to fix, like ticket routing.
questions.distractor_summary: Mortgages, medication, and layoffs significantly affect people and need meaningful human oversight.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: An insurance chatbot answers routine policy questions well but sometimes gets complex claims disputes wrong. What design best balances automation and safety?
options: Remove the chatbot entirely from the website of the insurer throughout the organization.
Set escalation rules so low-confidence answers and sensitive topics go to human agents
Raise the temperature so that the chatbot tries harder on disputes across the subscriptions.
Let the chatbot handle everything and review a sample once a year across the subscriptions.
questions.correct_rationale: Escalation paths triggered by confidence scores, topic detection, or customer requests let AI handle routine volume while people handle complex or sensitive cases.
questions.distractor_summary: Removing the chatbot gives up value, temperature doesn't fix judgment, and yearly sampling is too infrequent.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: A bank's customer assistant must never give personalized investment advice, must block abusive language, and must mask account numbers in its responses. Which Amazon Bedrock capability is designed to enforce these rules across applications?
options: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, which connect models to company data in the near term.
Provisioned Throughput, which reserves dedicated model capacity for this team.
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails: denied topics, content filters, and PII filters
AWS Cost Explorer, which shows the spending on AWS services
questions.correct_rationale: Bedrock Guardrails applies configurable safeguards: denied topics (such as investment advice), content filters for harmful or abusive content, PII redaction, and grounding checks.
questions.distractor_summary: Knowledge Bases provides RAG, Provisioned Throughput is a pricing and capacity option, and Cost Explorer analyzes spending.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: A retailer's new AI pricing engine starts setting obviously wrong prices on popular products during a holiday weekend. What safeguard should already have been in place?
options: A kill switch and rollback plan to disable the AI and revert to old pricing rules
A larger model that makes fewer mistakes in the prices that it sets
More marketing about the AI pricing engine of the retailer on holidays as a result over time.
Removing all of the monitoring, to reduce the noise over the weekend
questions.correct_rationale: Controllability includes the ability to stop and roll back AI quickly, with a tested fallback process.
questions.distractor_summary: A larger model doesn't stop the current failure, marketing doesn't fix it, and removing monitoring delays detection.

questions.domain: 3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
questions.question: A generative AI tool drafts 50,000 customer emails a month, and reviewing every one isn't feasible. How should the company maintain quality oversight?
options: Review none of the emails, since AI is reliable enough for this job
Review all 50,000 of the emails by hand each month, one by one
Stop using AI for the emails of the customers of the company
Regularly review a meaningful sample with automated checks, and sample more if issues appear
questions.correct_rationale: Human review by sampling, backed by automated quality and safety checks, scales oversight in proportion to risk and volume.
questions.distractor_summary: No review gives up quality assurance, full review removes the efficiency gain, and stopping gives up the value.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: Before committing $5 million to an enterprise AI program, a CEO wants to understand whether the organization is prepared. What should be assessed?
options: Only the IT infrastructure of the organization throughout the organization in production.
Readiness across strategy, people, processes, data, technology, culture, and governance
Only the size of the budget of the program throughout the organization for the application.
Only the announcements of the competitors about AI throughout the organization as needed.
questions.correct_rationale: AI readiness is multidimensional.
questions.distractor_summary: Gaps in leadership, skills, data, culture, or governance often derail programs more than technology gaps do. Looking only at infrastructure, budget, or competitors misses most failure points.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A company has run six generative AI experiments across departments. None are in production, and there are no shared platforms, standards, or governance. Where is it on a typical AI maturity curve, and what's the next focus?
options: Transforming; focus on new business models for the industry
Scaling; expand the experiments to all of the departments now
Experimenting or piloting; move the best use cases into production with shared foundations
Not started; begin with a first set of experiments next year
questions.correct_rationale: Isolated experiments with nothing in production and no common foundations mark an early stage.
questions.distractor_summary: The next step is to operationalize: take promising use cases to production while building reusable platforms, standards, and governance. Transformation and scaling come later, and the company has already started.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A readiness assessment shows a retailer has strong data but no one with experience evaluating generative AI outputs, managing AI vendors, or running AI products. What are the main ways to close this capability gap?
options: Combine options: train staff, hire key roles, and partner with knowledge transfer
Ignore it, since the technology will manage itself over the coming years for this team.
Only hire new people, and only after the program has finished entirely
Outsource all of the AI decision-making of the retailer for good, to a vendor in the near term.
questions.correct_rationale: Capability gaps are usually closed with a mix of upskilling, targeted hiring, and partnering, often at the same time, while building internal ownership.
questions.distractor_summary: Ignoring the gap, hiring too late, or outsourcing accountability permanently all undermine success.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: At a conservative financial firm, employees say failed projects have hurt careers in the past. Teams are reluctant to try AI experiments that might not work. What readiness issue is this, and what helps?
options: A data quality issue; clean the data of the firm before any experiment runs
A culture issue; leaders should create psychological safety, reward learning, and set guardrails
A model size issue; buy a bigger model for the teams to use at the firm
A budget issue; double the IT budget of the firm for this coming year
questions.correct_rationale: Culture is often the real blocker.
questions.distractor_summary: AI adoption needs experimentation within safe boundaries, so leaders must signal that disciplined experiments that "fail fast" are valued. Data, model size, and budget don't address fear of failure.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: After assessing current AI capabilities against the target state needed for its strategy, a company has a list of gaps in skills, data platforms, and governance. What should it do with this gap analysis?
options: File it away for the annual report of the company throughout the organization across the subscriptions.
Close every one of the gaps before starting any AI use case throughout the organization in every region.
Turn it into a sequenced roadmap that addresses foundational gaps alongside early, feasible use cases
Share it only with the IT department of the company throughout the organization across the subscriptions.
questions.correct_rationale: Gap analysis feeds the roadmap.
questions.distractor_summary: Effective roadmaps build foundations, such as data, skills, and governance, *in parallel* with quick-win use cases that deliver value and fund further investment. Filing it away wastes it, waiting for perfect readiness stalls progress, and gaps span the whole business, not just IT.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A company has four AI use cases in production with monitoring and a basic governance process. Each one was built separately, with its own data pipelines, prompts, and guardrails, which slows every new project. What's the logical next step in its AI maturity?
options: Return to experimenting with new proofs of concept for the business
Stop all of the new AI work until the next fiscal year begins
Replace all four use cases with one large model for the whole company
Scale with shared, reusable components (pipelines, guardrails, evaluations) and standards
questions.correct_rationale: Moving from "operationalizing" to "scaling" means turning one-off builds into reusable platforms and standards, so each new use case is faster and cheaper.
questions.distractor_summary: Going back to experiments or stopping loses momentum, and a single model doesn't solve the platform and process gap.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A telecom company wants AI to predict which customers will cancel. Customer profiles live in the CRM, billing history in a separate finance system, and support tickets in a third tool, and the systems don't share customer IDs. What's the main readiness problem?
options: The foundation model is too small for the customer data of the company
Data silos prevent a unified customer view; the data must be integrated and matched first
The company has too much data for a prediction model to use
The cloud Region that the company has chosen is the wrong one
questions.correct_rationale: Data silos are one of the most common blockers to AI value.
questions.distractor_summary: Predicting cancellations needs a combined view across systems with consistent identifiers. Model size, data volume, and Region aren't the issue.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: Three AI projects at a retailer keep failing because product attributes are inconsistent and outdated. When asked who maintains product data, each department points to another. What foundational step addresses the root cause?
options: Buy a larger AI model that can handle the messy data throughout the organization by default.
Have each AI project clean the product data separately throughout the organization in Azure.
Assign clear data ownership and stewardship, with accountable owners and quality standards
Stop using the product data in AI altogether throughout the organization for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: Without ownership, data quality decays and every project pays to clean the same data again.
questions.distractor_summary: Data governance roles, an owner who is accountable and stewards who maintain quality, fix the cause. Bigger models don't fix bad data, cleaning separately duplicates effort, and avoiding the data gives up value.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: Analysts at an insurer spend weeks finding out which data sets exist, what fields mean, and whether the data can be trusted before every AI project. What would help most?
options: A data catalog: a searchable inventory of data assets with owners and quality notes
More printed spreadsheets of the data sets for the analysts to read at this stage in the near term.
A larger context window for the model that the analysts already use
Asking the IT department to email the data sets on request each time in this case for the company.
questions.correct_rationale: A data catalog makes data discoverable, understandable, and trustworthy, cutting the time it takes to start AI work.
questions.distractor_summary: Printed spreadsheets and email requests don't scale, and a model's context window has nothing to do with finding data.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: An auditor asks a bank where the data used to train its credit model came from, and what transformations were applied before training. Which data capability answers this?
options: Data compression, which reduces the size of stored data
Model temperature, which controls the randomness of the output
Data minimization, which limits the data to what is needed
Data lineage: tracking the origin of the data and every change it went through
questions.correct_rationale: Data lineage records where data came from and how it changed.
questions.distractor_summary: It's essential for auditability, debugging, and regulatory trust in AI. Compression is about storage, temperature is a generation setting, and minimization limits what data is used.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A company plans a RAG assistant over its internal document repository. A sample review finds many outdated policies, several conflicting versions of the same document, and draft files mixed with final ones. What should happen before launch?
options: Launch now; the model will work out which of the versions is correct
Curate the sources: archive outdated and duplicate files, and assign content owners
Raise the temperature of the model to handle the ambiguity in the files for the company.
Fine-tune the model on all of the documents, including the drafts of them in this case.
questions.correct_rationale: RAG answers are only as good as the documents retrieved.
questions.distractor_summary: Conflicting or stale content produces confident wrong answers. Data readiness for generative AI includes curating unstructured content and giving it owners. The model can't reliably pick the right version, temperature doesn't help, and fine-tuning on drafts makes things worse.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A retailer wants AI to adjust promotions daily based on stock levels, but inventory data is loaded into its analytics platform only once a quarter. Which data-quality dimension is the problem?
options: Accuracy, which means the data is correct
Completeness, which means no values are missing for the team.
Timeliness (freshness), which means the data is up to date
Uniqueness, which means records are not duplicated in Azure.
questions.correct_rationale: Timeliness means data is current enough for its purpose.
questions.distractor_summary: Daily decisions can't rely on quarterly data, so the data pipeline must be updated to refresh more often. The data may well be accurate, complete, and free of duplicates and still be too old to use.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A company expects its AI workloads to grow, but it's unsure by how much. The IT director proposes spending $4 million upfront on on-premises GPU servers. What's the stronger infrastructure approach for this uncertainty?
options: Buy twice as many servers as needed, to be safe against growth
Delay all of the AI work until the demand is known for sure
Build a private data center that is used for AI work only
Use scalable cloud AI services with pay-as-you-go pricing, adding commitments later
questions.correct_rationale: With uncertain demand, elastic cloud resources and managed services avoid large upfront bets and idle capacity.
questions.distractor_summary: Savings Plans or provisioned capacity can be added once usage becomes predictable. Overbuying, delaying, or building a data center all lock in cost or give up value.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: An organization wants a central, scalable place to store structured and unstructured data of any type, such as documents, images, logs, and tables, as a foundation for analytics and AI on AWS. What is this commonly called, and which service typically underpins it?
options: A data lake, typically built on Amazon S3
A spreadsheet, built on Amazon Polly
A chatbot, built on Amazon Lex
A data silo, built on personal drives
questions.correct_rationale: A data lake centralizes raw data of any type at scale, and on AWS it's commonly built on Amazon S3, a common foundation for analytics and AI.
questions.distractor_summary: Polly is text-to-speech, Lex builds chatbots, and silos are the problem a data lake helps solve.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A CIO says, "No AI projects until our three-year enterprise data platform program is finished, because our data isn't ready." Meanwhile, two high-value use cases need only a few data sets that could be cleaned within two months. What's the best recommendation?
options: Agree, and pause all of the AI work of the company for three years
Prepare the data that priority use cases need now, and feed the lessons into the platform program
Launch AI on the current, uncleaned data across the whole company at once
Cancel the data platform program and focus the company only on AI
questions.correct_rationale: Data readiness can grow step by step, use case by use case.
questions.distractor_summary: Fixing the data that high-value use cases need delivers value early and guides the larger platform work. Waiting three years gives up value, using unclean data invites failure, and cancelling the platform program sacrifices long-term foundations.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: Research on AI programs consistently identifies one role as among the strongest predictors of success. Which role is it, and what does it do?
options: An external vendor who writes all of the code for the initiative
A junior analyst who documents the meetings of the project team
An executive sponsor who champions the work, secures funding, and removes roadblocks
A help-desk agent who answers the questions of the users every day as a result over time.
questions.correct_rationale: Executive sponsors give AI programs authority, resources, cross-functional alignment, and visible commitment, which are critical for overcoming resistance and scaling.
questions.distractor_summary: The other roles matter, but they can't provide that organizational leverage.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: After an AI document-processing tool is announced, back-office staff fear for their jobs. Some quietly avoid using it. What's the most effective leadership response?
options: Require usage of the tool and monitor every keystroke of the staff
Say nothing and hope that the fear of the staff fades over time
Promise that no role will ever change, even though that isn't true
Communicate openly how roles will change, involve staff in the redesign, and offer reskilling
questions.correct_rationale: Resistance often comes from uncertainty and fear.
questions.distractor_summary: Honest, transparent communication, involving staff in the redesign, and real reskilling investment build trust and adoption. Coercion breeds hidden resistance, silence feeds rumors, and false promises damage credibility.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A global company wants adoption of its new AI assistant to spread across 40 offices. A central training team alone can't reach everyone effectively. Which approach helps most?
options: An AI champions network: trained staff in each team who model usage and share feedback
A single company-wide email announcement from the chief executive to all for this team as a result.
A mandate with penalties for the staff who do not use the tool at all
Waiting for the employees to discover the tool by themselves over time over time in practice.
questions.correct_rationale: Peer champions inside teams spread practical know-how, build credibility, and surface feedback, and peer influence often beats top-down mandates.
questions.distractor_summary: One email doesn't change behavior, penalties breed resentment, and passive discovery leads to low adoption.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A company is designing an AI literacy program for 8,000 employees. Which approach is most effective?
options: The same three-day technical course for every one of the employees
Training only for the data scientists and engineers of the company
Role-based paths: baseline literacy for all, risk for leaders, deeper skills for builders
A one-hour video for all of the employees with no follow-up
questions.correct_rationale: Different roles need different depths.
questions.distractor_summary: Everyone needs basic literacy and safe-use rules, leaders need to understand strategy, value, and risk, and builders need technical depth. One-size-fits-all courses waste time, training only specialists leaves most users unprepared, and a single video doesn't build lasting skills.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: An IT team built an AI scheduling tool for field technicians without talking to them. At launch, technicians found it ignored real constraints such as traffic patterns and parts availability, and adoption collapsed. What would have prevented this?
options: A bigger launch event for the new tool with the technicians
A more advanced model for the scheduling tool of the company
Mandatory use of the tool that is enforced by the managers
Involving end users early in discovery, design, and pilots so the tool fits their work
questions.correct_rationale: Adoption depends on fit with real work.
questions.distractor_summary: Involving users early surfaces constraints, builds ownership, and creates champions. Launch events, more advanced models, and mandates don't fix a solution that doesn't match how the work is actually done.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A company will roll out generative AI tools to all employees over six months. What should its communication plan emphasize?
options: A single announcement on the launch day only, sent by email to all staff at this stage.
Regular, honest updates by audience: why, what it means, and how support works
Communication only to the senior leadership of the company in a briefing in the near term.
Technical details of the model architecture for all of the employees
questions.correct_rationale: Effective change communication is repeated, honest, and tailored.
questions.distractor_summary: It explains the "why," what's in it for each audience, and the support available, and it shows that feedback matters. One-time announcements, leadership-only updates, and deep technical detail don't drive adoption.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A logistics company is staffing the team for its first production AI initiative, an AI-assisted freight quoting tool. Which team composition is most likely to succeed?
options: Data scientists only, working in a separate team from the sales staff
IT infrastructure staff only, working in a separate team from the sales staff
A cross-functional team: business owner, sales users, tech specialists, and legal advisors
An external vendor working with no internal involvement at all
questions.correct_rationale: AI initiatives succeed when business, user, data, technical, and risk perspectives work together from the start.
questions.distractor_summary: Single-discipline teams miss either business fit or technical feasibility, and fully outsourced work leaves the company without internal ownership.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: In an AI initiative, who should play the product owner role, and what's its main responsibility?
options: A business leader accountable for the product's value, who prioritizes and decides trade-offs
The vendor's account manager, who works to maximize license sales for the vendor over time in practice.
The newest member of the team, who takes the notes in the meetings
The infrastructure engineer, who chooses the sizes of the servers for it
questions.correct_rationale: A product owner from the business keeps the AI work tied to outcomes, prioritizes the backlog, and makes value trade-offs.
questions.distractor_summary: Vendors have their own incentives, note-taking isn't ownership, and infrastructure sizing is a technical task.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: Three months after buying 2,000 licenses for an AI assistant, usage data shows only 400 people use it weekly. What's the most effective next step?
options: Cancel the program immediately and ask the vendor for a refund
Buy 2,000 more licenses to increase the visibility of the tool
Assume that the other 1,600 people will start to use it eventually over time in practice.
Find the barriers through interviews and usage data, then offer targeted training
questions.correct_rationale: Low adoption is a signal to diagnose, not to ignore or overreact to.
questions.distractor_summary: Common causes are unclear use cases, lack of skills, poor workflow fit, or trust concerns, and each needs a targeted fix. Cancelling too early wastes the investment, buying more licenses adds cost, and waiting rarely changes behavior.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A successful pilot of an AI claims assistant in one region is approved for scaling to 12 regions. Which rollout approach best manages risk?
options: Launch in all 12 regions on the same day to save time and effort as a result.
A phased rollout in waves, using the lessons of each wave before the next
Roll out only to the region of the CEO and keep it there forever
Restart from a new proof of concept in each one of the 12 regions for this team.
questions.correct_rationale: Phased rollouts limit the damage if issues arise and allow learning and adjustment between waves.
questions.distractor_summary: Big-bang launches magnify problems, staying in one region forever gives up value, and repeating proofs of concept wastes proven work.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A pilot AI tool ran well for 50 users on a team-managed setup with no formal support. Leadership wants it available to 5,000 employees next month. What must be addressed before scaling?
options: Nothing at all, since the pilot worked well for the 50 users of the team
Only the colors of the user interface of the tool of the team
Production readiness: security, access controls, monitoring, support, and scale testing
A new marketing name for the tool of the company before the launch
questions.correct_rationale: A pilot isn't production.
questions.distractor_summary: Scaling 100 times exposes gaps in security, reliability, support, and cost that a small pilot hides. Interface colors and names don't affect readiness, and assuming the pilot setup will hold invites outages and incidents.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A bank's AI team notices each new generative AI use case takes four months, mostly because it rebuilds data connectors, guardrails, and evaluation tests from scratch. What would most speed up scaling?
options: A shared AI platform of reusable parts: model access, guardrails, templates, and evaluations
Hiring more people to rebuild the same components faster for each use case over time in practice.
Skipping the guardrails and the evaluation for the new use cases of the bank for this team as a result.
Limiting the bank to one AI use case at a time for the whole year
questions.correct_rationale: Reusable platforms lower the cost and time of each new use case and keep governance consistent.
questions.distractor_summary: More people rebuilding the same things doesn't scale, skipping safeguards creates risk, and capping the number of use cases limits value.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A large company wants AI expertise and standards set centrally, while business units build and own their own use cases close to their customers. Which operating model is this?
options: Fully centralized, with all of the work done by one central team at this stage in the near term.
Fully decentralized, with each business unit working on its own for this team as a result over time.
Outsourced, with all of the AI work done by an outside vendor in practice in this case for the company.
Hub-and-spoke (federated): a central hub sets standards, and spokes deliver in the units
questions.correct_rationale: Hub-and-spoke combines central consistency (standards, platforms, governance, expertise) with local speed and business ownership.
questions.distractor_summary: Fully centralized models often become bottlenecks, fully decentralized ones duplicate effort and create inconsistent risk, and outsourcing gives up ownership.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A program director proposes building a full enterprise AI solution over 18 months and launching it all at once. What approach does the AI strategist recommend instead?
options: Make the 18-month plan 36 months long, to be on the safe side
An iterative approach: short cycles, measured outcomes, feedback, and adjustment
Wait for the AI technology to stop changing before the project starts for the company.
Launch a minimal version of the solution with no measurement of the results in this case.
questions.correct_rationale: Iterative delivery reduces risk, delivers value sooner, and adapts to fast-moving technology and user feedback.
questions.distractor_summary: Longer big-bang plans raise the risk of building the wrong thing, waiting for stability never ends, and launching without measurement prevents learning.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A generative AI document assistant cost $3,000 a month during its pilot. Scaling to the whole company will raise volume about 50 times, which would cost $150,000 a month at current per-request costs and erase the business case. What should the team do?
options: Cancel the scale-up of the document assistant to the whole company
Scale anyway and hope that the prices of the models fall in the future
Revisit unit economics: right-size the model, cut tokens, batch work, and consider commitments
Reduce the number of users who are allowed once the scale-up has happened
questions.correct_rationale: Costs that are tolerable in a pilot can break at scale.
questions.distractor_summary: Cost optimization levers often cut unit costs dramatically: smaller models, token efficiency, batch processing, and pricing commitments. Cancelling gives up value, hoping for price drops isn't a plan, and restricting users undermines the reason for scaling.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A conglomerate's eight business units each picked their own AI vendors, guardrails, and data practices. Leadership now finds duplicate contracts, inconsistent risk controls, and no way to share successful solutions. What's the core issue?
options: Too much central control by the head office of the conglomerate
Decentralization with no shared standards or platforms, causing duplication and inconsistent risk
Too few AI tools at the business units of the conglomerate today
The business units are too small to run AI projects on their own
questions.correct_rationale: Fully decentralized AI adoption gives speed at first but leads to duplicated spending, uneven risk controls, and lost reuse.
questions.distractor_summary: A federated model with shared standards and platforms fixes this while keeping local ownership. The problem isn't too much control, too few tools, or unit size.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A US retailer's AI product-recommendation engine succeeded domestically. The company wants to scale it to the EU and Japan next quarter. Beyond technical deployment, what must be reassessed?
options: Nothing, because the model already works well in the United States in practice in this case.
Only the currency format of the prices of the products on the site
Only the server capacity in the new regions of the company
Regulation, privacy, data residency, consent, language, and fit of the training data
questions.correct_rationale: Scaling across borders brings new laws (such as GDPR and the EU AI Act), new data residency and consent needs, language and cultural differences, and customer data the model wasn't trained on.
questions.distractor_summary: Each of these can affect compliance, fairness, and performance. Currency and capacity are only part of the picture.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: What's the main purpose of an AI Center of Excellence (CoE)?
options: To set standards, share reusable assets, build skills, and help teams adopt AI safely
To personally approve and build every one of the AI projects in the company in the near term.
To replace all of the decision-making of the business units about AI
To manage the IT hardware that is used in the offices of the company
questions.correct_rationale: An AI CoE speeds up and standardizes adoption through expertise, guidance, enablement, and reusable assets.
questions.distractor_summary: It shouldn't become the only gatekeeper or builder, take over business ownership, or handle unrelated IT tasks.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: Two years in, a company's AI CoE has a nine-month backlog because every AI request must be built by the CoE's eight people. Business units are frustrated and some are going around it. What change makes sense?
options: Disband the CoE and let every team do whatever it wants with AI
Double the backlog limit of the CoE to make the queue look shorter
Shift toward enablement: platforms, guardrails, templates, and training for business teams
Require that all of the requests wait in line, regardless of their value
questions.correct_rationale: As maturity grows, CoEs should move from doing everything to enabling others through self-service platforms and standards, which scales capacity without losing governance.
questions.distractor_summary: Disbanding loses standards, and longer backlogs or rigid queues worsen the bottleneck and encourage shadow AI.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: An AI customer-service assistant met its targets at launch. A year later, satisfaction has slowly declined because products, policies, and customer questions changed while the assistant didn't. What practice was missing?
options: A bigger launch budget for the assistant of the support team
Continuous improvement: review metrics and feedback, update content and prompts, and re-measure
A one-time survey of the customers after the launch of the assistant
Replacing the assistant every year with a new one from a vendor
questions.correct_rationale: AI programs are never "done." Continuous improvement loops keep solutions aligned with changing products, policies, and users.
questions.distractor_summary: Launch budgets don't sustain value, a single survey is a snapshot, and yearly replacement is costly and unnecessary.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: The board asks the Chief AI Officer for a quarterly view of whether the enterprise AI program is working. Which set of program-level metrics is most appropriate?
options: The number of AI-related meetings that were held during the quarter in the near term for this team.
The number of AI vendors that the company has contacted this year as a result over time in practice.
The total GPU hours consumed, with no other context for the board
Value against targets, use cases in production, adoption, risk trends, and capability progress
questions.correct_rationale: Boards need outcome-focused metrics that cover value, scale, adoption, risk, and capability building.
questions.distractor_summary: Activity counts such as meetings and vendors contacted, or raw usage without context, don't show whether the program is creating value responsibly.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A company finds that teams in different divisions keep making the same mistakes on AI projects: underestimating data cleanup, skipping baselines, and launching without change plans. What practice would help most?
options: Systematic knowledge sharing: lessons repository, playbooks, communities, and project reviews
Keeping the lessons of each project confidential within its own team
Blaming the teams that made the mistakes on the earlier projects
Stopping all of the new AI projects of the company for a year
questions.correct_rationale: Organizational learning turns individual project experience into shared playbooks and patterns, reducing repeated mistakes and speeding up delivery.
questions.distractor_summary: Secrecy and blame discourage learning, and stopping projects gives up value.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: A company's innovation funnel shows that out of 120 AI ideas submitted last year, 30 became proofs of concept, 10 became pilots, and 4 scaled to production with measurable value. How should leadership read this?
options: The program has failed, because most of the ideas didn't scale up in practice in this case.
Only 4 ideas should have been submitted by the staff in the year for the company at this stage.
A healthy funnel: many ideas, disciplined filtering, early stops, and focus on winners
Every one of the ideas should have been scaled to production in the near term for this team.
questions.correct_rationale: A healthy AI portfolio deliberately stops most ideas early and cheaply, and puts investment into the few that prove value.
questions.distractor_summary: That's disciplined portfolio management, not failure. Limiting submissions reduces options, and scaling everything wastes resources on weak use cases.

questions.domain: 4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
questions.question: After a successful AI launch, the project team was disbanded and no one was assigned to the solution. Eighteen months later, usage and value have quietly eroded. What does sustaining AI value require?
options: A new launch event every year for the solution and its users
Ongoing ownership: an accountable owner, support, value monitoring, and user reinforcement
Removing the metrics of the solution so that the decline isn't visible as a result over time.
A larger initial project budget for the solution at the start
questions.correct_rationale: Value lasts only with continued ownership, monitoring, and reinforcement, the "Reinforcement" step in change models such as ADKAR.
questions.distractor_summary: Launch events, hidden metrics, and bigger initial budgets don't replace accountability after launch.
